KYC vs AML: how KYC fits inside an AML program

MT

Mehak Tariq, CAMSNovember 27, 2026•8 min read

KYC (know your customer) is the work a bank does to identify, verify and understand each customer. AML (anti-money laundering) is the wider program a bank runs to prevent, detect and report money laundering and terrorist financing, and KYC is one part of it. Under the US Bank Secrecy Act rules, the customer identification program "must be a part of the anti-money laundering compliance program", in the words of 31 CFR 1020.220.

This guide sets out what each side covers for a US bank, the differences in one table, how KYC information becomes the baseline for monitoring, and how a compliance team runs KYC and AML work as one process. It explains public guidance and is not legal advice.

What KYC covers at a bank

In US rules, the parts usually grouped as KYC are spread across three regulations. Our guide to KYC covers each one in more depth.

  • The customer identification program (CIP) in 31 CFR 1020.220. Before opening an account the bank must obtain, at a minimum, the customer's name, date of birth for an individual, address and an identification number. Its procedures must let it "form a reasonable belief that it knows the true identity of each customer", and verification happens "within a reasonable time after the account is opened". The CIP also has to check whether the customer appears on a federal government list of known or suspected terrorists or terrorist organizations.
  • Beneficial ownership in 31 CFR 1010.230. For a legal entity customer, the bank identifies each individual who owns 25 percent or more of the equity interests and a single individual with significant responsibility to control, manage or direct the company, such as a CEO or CFO.
  • Customer due diligence (CDD) in the AML program rule, 31 CFR 1020.210. The bank must understand "the nature and purpose of customer relationships for the purpose of developing a customer risk profile".

The identity checks themselves are covered in our post on KYC verification.

What an AML program covers

The AML program is set by 31 CFR 1020.210. For a bank with a federal functional regulator, the program must include, at a minimum:

  1. a system of internal controls to assure ongoing compliance;
  2. independent testing for compliance, by bank staff or an outside party;
  3. one or more named individuals responsible for coordinating and monitoring day-to-day compliance;
  4. training for appropriate personnel;
  5. risk-based procedures for ongoing customer due diligence, which include the customer risk profile and "ongoing monitoring to identify and report suspicious transactions and, on a risk basis, to maintain and update customer information".

The program must also meet the due diligence rules for correspondent accounts for foreign financial institutions in 31 CFR 1010.610 and for private banking accounts in 31 CFR 1010.620. The BSA/AML manual of the Federal Financial Institutions Examination Council (FFIEC) adds that the program must be written, approved by the board of directors and noted in the board minutes, and that "written policies, procedures, and processes alone are not sufficient". The bank needs practices that match them.

The program sits alongside the BSA reporting rules. A bank files a suspicious activity report under 31 CFR 1020.320 for a transaction that involves or aggregates at least $5,000 when it knows, suspects or has reason to suspect that the transaction meets one of the rule's conditions, such as involving funds from illegal activity. The report is generally due no later than 30 calendar days after initial detection. It files a currency transaction report for each transaction in currency of more than $10,000 under 31 CFR 1010.311; our currency transaction report guide walks through that filing. The FFIEC manual also notes that customer information collected under the CDD rule may be relevant to determining parties sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), which is where sanctions screening comes in.

KYC vs AML at a glance

KYCAML program
Main questionWho is this customer, who owns and controls it, and what is the relationship for?Is the bank being used, across all its customers, to launder money or finance terrorism, and is suspicious activity reported?
Core rules31 CFR 1020.220 (CIP), 1010.230 (beneficial owners), the CDD element of 1020.21031 CFR 1020.210 (program), 1020.320 (SARs), 1010.311 (CTRs), plus the KYC rules
When it runsAt account opening, then when monitoring shows customer information has changedFor the whole life of every relationship
What it producesVerified identity, ownership records and a customer risk profileAlerts, investigations, SAR and CTR filings, testing and training records
ScopeOne customer at a timeThe bank as a whole, including governance and staff

The KYC side supplies the facts about each customer, and the rest of the AML program acts on them.

How KYC information feeds AML monitoring

The FFIEC manual's customer due diligence section says "the cornerstone of a strong BSA/AML compliance program" is risk-based CDD policies, procedures and processes for all customers. The bank "is expected to use the customer information and customer risk profile in its suspicious activity monitoring process" to understand what a customer would normally be expected to do, as "a baseline against which suspicious transactions are identified".

The manual warns that getting a customer's risk wrong "can have a cascading effect", "creating deficiencies in multiple areas of internal controls". Monitoring compares each customer's activity with the expected activity recorded in the customer file. If a business customer's file records modest monthly volumes and the account suddenly handles far more, monitoring should flag the gap against the expected activity in the file.

Monitoring also feeds KYC. The manual says: "The requirement to update customer information is event-driven and occurs as a result of normal monitoring." When monitoring shows that customer information has materially changed, the bank should update it and, where it matters to the risk, reassess the customer risk profile. The manual lists factors that can prompt a review:

  • significant and unexplained changes in account activity;
  • changes in employment or business operation;
  • changes in ownership of a business entity;
  • red flags identified through suspicious activity monitoring;
  • law enforcement inquiries and requests, such as criminal subpoenas, National Security Letters and section 314(a) requests;
  • results of negative media searches;
  • the length of time since customer information was gathered and the risk profile assessed.

The manual is also clear that this element "does not impose a categorical requirement" to update customer information on a continuous or periodic basis. A bank may still set risk-based periodic reviews in its own procedures, which is where a periodic KYC review comes in.

How a bank or fintech team runs KYC and AML together

A team that runs KYC and AML work as one loop usually works through these steps:

  1. Collect the CIP information before the account opens. Name, date of birth, address and identification number are the minimum; the procedure says which documents or non-documentary methods the bank uses to verify them.
  2. Verify identity, check the government lists within a reasonable period after the account is opened, and record what was relied on and the result.
  3. For a business customer, identify the beneficial owners at the 25 percent threshold and the control person. The manual notes this information is collected at that threshold "regardless of the customer's risk profile".
  4. Build the customer risk profile from the nature and purpose of the relationship, looking at products and services, the type of customer and geography. For higher-risk customers, collect more, such as source of funds and wealth or expected transaction volumes. That extra work is enhanced due diligence.
  5. Use the same customer and ownership information for sanctions screening, and set the risk profile as the monitoring baseline.
  6. Work monitoring alerts against that baseline. Each alert is cleared or escalated to an investigation. Where a SAR is warranted, it is generally due no later than 30 calendar days after the bank first detects facts that may support filing. Our AML case management guide follows a case from alert to decision.
  7. Send what monitoring learns back to KYC. Update the customer information, reassess the risk profile, and record who changed it. The manual expects procedures to say who is authorized to change a customer's risk profile.
  8. Keep the records. CIP identifying information is kept for five years after the account is closed, and the verification records for five years after they are made.

Steps 1 to 5 are usually called KYC, steps 6 and 7 AML, and step 8 applies to both. The hand-offs between them are where the customer record has to stay current. Tools for KYC automation and AML automation can keep both sides working from the same customer record. Verkflo, for example, runs a team's written KYC and AML procedures as versioned agent workflows that pause for human review where the procedure says so and record each step in an audit log.

Where fintechs fit

A fintech that is a money services business has its own program rule in 31 CFR 1022.210, which requires a written, "effective anti-money laundering program" that is "reasonably designed to prevent the money services business from being used to facilitate money laundering". A fintech that serves customers through a partner bank should confirm in writing which KYC and AML steps it runs and which the bank runs, because the bank's program still has to meet its own rules.

Proposed changes to the CDD rule

On November 17, 2026, FinCEN issued a proposed rule to strengthen customer due diligence requirements, as part of Treasury's implementation of Executive Order 14406, Restoring Integrity to America's Financial System. It is a proposal, so the current rule text still applies.

Common questions

Is KYC part of AML?

Yes. The CIP rule says the CIP must be part of the AML compliance program, and ongoing customer due diligence is one of the minimum elements of the bank AML program rule.

Which comes first, KYC or AML?

KYC starts first, because the bank collects identifying information before it opens the account. AML monitoring then runs for the life of the relationship and feeds changes back into the customer file.

Does KYC have to be refreshed on a fixed schedule?

Not under the CDD rule. The FFIEC manual says the update requirement is event-driven, though a bank may set risk-based periodic reviews in its own procedures.

What are the minimum parts of a bank AML program?

Under 31 CFR 1020.210: internal controls, independent testing, a named person or people responsible for day-to-day compliance, training, and risk-based procedures for ongoing customer due diligence. The program must also comply with 31 CFR 1010.610 and 1010.620.
